title: Agent guide
body:
# Agent guide

Call `get_guide` on connection and after each learning step. Use the Next Step and the learner’s goal to choose a workflow.

1. **Start together.** Read [how Startodel works](startodel://guide/platform), then [complete the Onboarding Questionnaire](startodel://guide/first-steps). Finish with a first Topic the learner recognizes as relevant.
2. **Plan a Track.** For a technology or comparison, [design and verify a Track](startodel://guide/build-track-technology). For a codebase, [pin the repository revision](startodel://guide/build-track-from-repo) first. Finish with a sourced Track Graph that leads to an agreed task or decision.
3. **Teach and assess.** [Choose the next Topic](startodel://guide/agent-workflow), [write a Lesson](startodel://guide/lessons-and-blocks) when needed, and [work through it with the learner](startodel://guide/user-workflow). For an oral or written assessment, [continue a GrillSession](startodel://guide/grill-session). For due Topics, [conduct a Review](startodel://guide/review-loop). Finish with the learner’s recorded evidence.

The eleven top-level Markdown files supply the MCP guide sections. The five installable skills combine their workflow sections with the [shared rules](startodel://guide/rules). Worked examples live under `references/` and open through a link in the relevant workflow. To install a skill, copy its whole folder recursively so its relative reference links resolve.

title: How Startodel works
body:
# How Startodel works

Call `get_guide` first. Use the learner’s Profile and goal to choose a Topic, teach its mechanism, then ask the learner to use it. Record their answer and evidence through the Tools. The MCP Token selects the Owner.

1. **Orient.** Read the Next Step and its reason. Use `get_progress` when choosing between studying, a GrillSession and due ReviewItems. Leave the learner with one activity they can start now.
2. **Locate the work.** A Topic lives once in the Owner’s Topic Catalog. Tracks order Topics, and TopicEdges connect prerequisites to dependents. Before teaching, identify the Topic whose Lessons and Mastery will carry across its Tracks.
3. **Close the loop.** Startodel scores Quizzes and schedules Reviews. You assess free-text Exercises and Grill Questions. Finish with the learner’s recorded result and the next action from `get_guide`.

title: Complete the Onboarding Questionnaire
body:
# Complete the Onboarding Questionnaire

On connection, call `get_guide`, then `get_profile`. Use `update_profile` to save the learner’s confirmed Onboarding Questionnaire answers.

1. **Connect.** If the learner needs access, have them issue an MCP Token in Settings and configure their client for Streamable HTTP at the installation’s `/mcp` URL with the Bearer credential in its secret input. Continue when `get_profile` returns the learner’s Profile.
2. **Fill the gaps.** Compare the saved stack, goals and grade with what you already know about the learner. Ask about a current project when it would clarify the goal. Save partial answers as they arrive. Finish when the learner recognizes the stack, goal and grade in your readback.
3. **Agree on a starting point.** Offer a first Topic and an example from their work in their preferred language. Confirm anything uncertain. Mark onboarding complete after the learner confirms the questionnaire, then read `get_guide` for the new Next Step.

title: Working with the learner
body:
# Working with the learner

Use `get_lesson` to teach in chat. After the learner acts, use `mark_lesson_read` for confirmed reading, `record_quiz_result` for their Quiz choices or `set_mastery` for demonstrated depth.

1. **Frame the Lesson.** Name something the learner wants to do in their project. Ask them to predict what a small example will do. Begin the explanation from the first point where their prediction and the trace diverge, or move to a harder case if they agree.
2. **Hear the reasoning.** Present Quiz prompts and options, then submit the learner’s own choices and discuss the returned feedback. For an Exercise, offer a hint and reveal the solution on explicit request. Finish with the learner’s explanation of what changed in their example.
3. **Record the result.** Capture confirmed reading or actual Quiz choices through the corresponding Tool. Mastery starts at 0. Reading all Lessons in a Topic with at least one Lesson raises it to 1. Fully correct latest Quiz Attempts on all Quizzes in a Topic with at least one Quiz raise it to 2. These automatic rules only raise Mastery. For free-text work, cite the learner’s words or trace. Finish with a saved result and a next Topic or practice task the learner can name.

title: Choose the next Topic
body:
# Choose the next Topic

Use `get_profile`, `get_progress`, `list_tracks` and `get_track_graph` to find a Topic that advances the learner’s goal. Inspect `get_topic` and `list_lessons` before deciding what to teach.

1. **Check readiness.** Choose a Topic below Mastery 2 whose prerequisites have all reached 2, including prerequisites outside this Track. When none qualifies, identify the blocking prerequisite, a cycle or a completed Track before proposing a next move.
2. **Match the learner.** Check the starting Topic and depth against their project and prior experience. Read an existing Lesson with `get_lesson`, or use the Lesson workflow to write one. Continue when the learner has a specific question they will be able to answer.
3. **Try a variation.** Change one input or constraint and ask the learner to predict the effect. Assess their explanation against the evidence rules, then call `get_guide` once the result is recorded.

title: Design and verify a Track
body:
# Design and verify a Track

Start with `get_profile` and `list_topics` to personalize the plan and find reusable Topics. After research and agreement on the outline, use `create_track`, `upsert_topics`, `add_edges` and `attach_topics_to_track`.

1. **Personalize the outcome.** Combine the Onboarding Questionnaire with what you know of the learner’s work. Name the task they want to perform, the starting Topic and a familiar example. Confirm the choice if their background or goal is uncertain.
2. **Verify the sources.** Before designing the Track, use your own web and repository tools to verify the current release and read a primary source for each technology. Check official documentation against recent release notes, a maintainer article or the primary repository. Proceed only when each design decision has a supporting source URL and its version or date.
3. **Choose a mode from the goal.** Agree on an outline that ends in an observable decision or working result.
   - **Comparison mode** for “How do X and Y differ?” Build a mental model of each, including its core problem and architecture. Apply both to the same case. Derive tradeoffs and decision criteria, then vary a constraint. End with a scenario-based Quiz asking which fits the new case, followed by “Why?” in chat.
   - **Deep-dive mode** for “Teach me X.” Connect a mental model to the learner’s concrete goal. Start with a working setup or configuration, trace the internals that explain its behavior, then diagnose a production failure. End with an Exercise where the learner changes the setup and verifies the result independently.
4. **Build and read back.** Reuse matching Topic Slugs. Create the private Track with verified citations in Track Sources and identify their versions or dates in the description. Save the missing Topics, connect prerequisites to dependents and attach members in teaching order. Check `get_track` for the citations and `get_track_graph` for the agreed first Topic and path to the outcome. The Track is ready when both match the plan.
5. **Revise an existing Track.** For a changed source or goal use `update_track`. For an incorrect prerequisite use `remove_edge`. For a Topic that no longer belongs use `detach_topic_from_track`, which preserves its Lessons. Verify the affected sources, edges or memberships on readback.

title: Build a Track from a repository
body:
# Build a Track from a repository

Use `get_profile` to establish the learner’s goal and `list_topics` to find relevant prior work. Ground the Track in a real repository revision before applying the Track design workflow.

1. **Pin the task.** Pair the learner’s project and experience with a change, diagnosis or design choice they want to make. Resolve the target release or branch to a commit. Continue when you can name the task and link to the revision.
2. **Trace one real call.** Use your own repository and web tools to check the release history and official docs against that revision. Follow a public entry point through its implementation to a test that exercises the behavior. Keep a permalink to each and distinguish the public guarantee from the implementation detail. If access is missing, get the source or a verifiable public revision before continuing.
3. **Choose the route.** Use comparison mode for a choice between approaches and deep-dive mode for a working change. For a comparison, trace the same operation on both sides. For a deep dive, locate the setup and a failure the learner can reproduce. Take those findings into the Track design workflow. The outline is ready to build when it names the mode, the pinned revision for the Track description and the permalinks for Track Sources.

title: Write a Lesson with Blocks
body:
# Write a Lesson with Blocks

Use `get_profile` to calibrate the Lesson. Inspect `list_lessons` and `get_lesson` for the Topic, then use `create_lesson` or `update_lesson` once the content meets the criteria below.

1. **Choose a prediction.** Use the learner’s current project and prior knowledge to pick a question they can test in their preferred language. Before writing the Lesson, use your own web and repository tools to verify the behavior against a current primary source. Record its version or date and the passage, test or implementation that supports the prediction.
2. **Teach the mechanism.** Write an original explanation of why the behavior follows from the mental model. Show a minimal runnable or traceable example. Give the starting state, the change and the expected observation so the learner can check the prediction.
3. **Make the caveat tangible.** Include a substantive Callout Block (`production`, `gotcha` or `tip`). Describe a production symptom or a non-obvious trick, the condition that causes it and one way to detect or address it. Cite the verified primary source in a Link Block or Video Block with its version or date and what to inspect.
4. **Test understanding.** Use a Quiz to apply the idea or diagnose a failure, or a transfer Exercise that changes a constraint and asks for a prediction, fix or trace. The learner should face a fresh case, with feedback that explains the decisive condition.
5. **Check the saved Lesson.** When replacing Blocks, retain the content and stable IDs the learner still needs. Read the Lesson back. It is ready only when the mechanism, example, substantive Callout, dated or versioned primary citation, and Quiz or Exercise are all present.

For a worked example of how all seven Blocks fit together, open the [browser tasks Lesson](startodel://guide/references/browser-tasks).

title: Continue a GrillSession
body:
# Continue a GrillSession

Use `get_profile` to set the level. Resume with `list_grills` and `get_grill`, or open a new GrillSession with `start_grill`. Check for stored answers before choosing the next question.

1. **Choose questions.** Use `get_grill_candidates` to choose due or weak Topics and `add_grill_questions` to save prompts linked to them. At the learner’s level, test recall, application and explanation. Start with a familiar project behavior, change one constraint, then ask why the prediction holds. Finish with an ordered set of prompts the learner can answer individually.
2. **Hear one answer.** Ask one Grill Question and wait. Use `submit_grill_answer` for the learner’s own chat or spoken response. For an answer already submitted in the app, use the text returned by `get_grill`. Continue once the question has a stored answer.
3. **Judge the reasoning.** Quote the part of the answer that determined the Verdict. Use `judge_grill_answer` to save the Verdict, quote and a specific correction or harder follow-up. The question is assessed when its stored answer has a Verdict and feedback, even if the GrillSession has since finished.
4. **Close the round.** Use `finish_grill` and discuss the weakest Topic or next challenge. A partial or weak Verdict already refreshes the linked ReviewItem. Finish with one practice task tied to the learner’s evidence.

title: Review due Topics
body:
# Review due Topics

Use `list_due_reviews` to choose a due ReviewItem and `get_profile` to calibrate practice. For an agent-led Review, record the Verdict with `record_review_result`. Use `set_mastery` for a change in demonstrated depth.

1. **Choose practice.** Read the due Topic and the last reason. For a Topic with Quizzes, offer the in-app Practice Quiz. Submission records Quiz Attempts and reschedules the ReviewItem. That branch ends with the returned result and next due time. For a free-text Review, agree on a task at the learner’s current level.
2. **Retrieve and transfer.** Test recall, application and explanation. Ask for the mental model from memory, then change one condition in a case from their stack and ask what happens and why. Wait for the learner’s own prediction and reasoning.
3. **Assess once.** Quote the part of the answer that determined the Verdict in the recorded reason. Tie the quoted reasoning to the shared strong, partial or weak criteria. Finish with one recorded ReviewItem update and its next due time.
4. **Choose the next challenge.** Use the shared Mastery criteria for evidence of greater depth. If the learner missed a condition, ask for a corrected prediction in a fresh case. End with a specific follow-up they can try before the next Review.

title: Rules for external agents
body:
# Rules for external agents

Call `get_guide` on connection and after each learning step. Use the returned Next Step and its reason to pick the workflow.

1. **Personalize first.** Use `get_profile` to combine the Onboarding Questionnaire with what you already know about the learner’s stack, experience, current project and preferred language. For someone new to the subject, teach foundations through a concrete analogy, explain jargon before use and add one step at a time. With an experienced developer, skip known foundations and bridge from a familiar concept to mechanisms and tradeoffs. Choose the starting Topic, depth, examples and language from that picture. If uncertain, confirm the choice with the learner. Start when you can name a first question in their preferred language.
2. **Record evidence.** Use the learner’s own answer. For free text, a strong Verdict means the answer addresses the prompt accurately, partial identifies a sound idea missing a material condition, and weak identifies faulty reasoning or an inability to apply the idea. Set Mastery 3 only with evidence that the learner explains the mechanism, or 4 with a trace of the internals. Save the specific evidence with `set_mastery`.
3. **Protect the Owner.** The MCP Token selects the Owner. Never pass User or Owner IDs to a Tool. Keep credentials out of prompts and learning records. If a token is lost, direct the learner to revoke it in Settings. Before a large rewrite, identify all affected Tracks and get the learner’s agreement. Preserve Topic Slugs and Block IDs across edits.
4. **Publish by request.** Tracks start private. Use `set_track_visibility` only when the learner explicitly requests that visibility change in this conversation. Publishing requires current Terms Acceptance in the app. If missing, direct the learner to the Track to accept the Publishing rules and Terms of Use. A Public Track shares Track Sources, member Topics and Lessons. Its public Lesson preview hides Quiz answers and Exercise solutions. A Fork starts private with working practice. Check the resulting visibility against the request.
